DR HUW MAYBERRY (recalled) (via video link)
Examination-in-chief by MR DRIVER
We'll see and recognise on screen Dr Huw Mayberry.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Dr Mayberry, can you see and hear me clearly?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, I can.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Good evening. I'm sure you appreciate --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Sorry?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It's not on the screen.
blocks.speaker: JUROR

blocks.text: Dr Mayberry, we're just ensuring that everyone can see your image on screen. A brief technical hitch.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: (Pause)
Dr Mayberry, do you appreciate that you are still bound by the affirmation that you took prior to giving evidence on the last occasion?
Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Thank you. This morning you're going to be asked questions in relation to your involvement in the care of a baby by the name of [Baby O].
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: We appreciate that, to a limited degree, you may also have had some contact with his brother, [Baby P], but for this morning's purposes we are focusing upon the baby [Baby O].
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Sure.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Were you working a night shift at the Countess of Chester Hospital on 22 June 2016?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: At some point overnight did you have direct involvement with the triplet [Baby O]?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Can you remember, in broad terms, what were the circumstances that led you to his cot side?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Sure. So I had a call from one of the nursing staff, I can't remember quite who, but Sophie Ellis, who was the nurse who was looking after [Baby O], had noted that his abdomen had become a little distended and so had asked me to see him.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Thank you. Upon receipt of that request, did you attend to his cot side within his nursery?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: I think it's right, for reasons that we'll come to in due course, you never actually made a note of your examination of [Baby O] within his clinical notes; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: This is correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Therefore it is a little difficult, do you agree, for us to pinpoint with accuracy the time at which you attended upon him?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That is correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: We'll go to your examination in a moment, forgive me, but in general terms can you explain to the jury why it was on this occasion, with this baby, that you didn't make notes immediately after your examination?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Sure. So I saw [Baby O], examined him, and then as I was about to go and write -- can you hear me okay, sorry?
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: There's a lot of feedback.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: We can.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: As I went to write his notes, I got bleeped away for an emergency for another child.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Thank you. What, if any, steps did you take to ensure that a note or a record was made of your examination?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I asked Sophie Ellis if she could just -- to make sure that there was a record, document, that I had seen the child, examined the abdomen and that I was happy that the abdomen was soft and was not concerning.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Even in those circumstances, if you'd discovered anything unusual or anything of concern or any exceptional feature in the presentation, would you have made a note or would you have just left it to Sophie Ellis?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: No. If I'd found anything concerning I (a) would have acted upon it and (b) would have ensured that I'd gone back and made a note.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Was there any particular event that causes you to specifically remember the fact of not making a note?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. On the next night shift that I came in, that night one of my colleagues had told me about what had happened to [Baby O]. I was obviously very shocked about the situation and then I remembered clearly that I'd seen him and that I felt that he was very well and I hadn't specifically documented that myself, even though I'd asked the nurse to.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Do you recall any discussion with any colleagues about the absence of a note?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I had subsequently spoken to Dr Brearey to say that I had not made a note about it and I had said at handover as well that I'd examined the child, they were well, but I hadn't had an opportunity to make a note because of the emergency I was called to.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Thank you. Let's then consider what you can remember of your examination of [Baby O]. You told us the reasons why you were invited to examine him. Could you now tell us what you discovered upon examination?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I discovered a child who was well in themselves. While their abdomen was mildly distended, it was entirely soft. [Baby O] had good reason to have a distended but soft abdomen, having been on previously continual positive airway pressure, noninvasive ventilation and subsequently high-flow nasal cannula, non-invasive ventilation.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: It's implicit from your use of the description "soft", but did you palpate the baby's abdomen?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Having examined him, what was your overall view of his condition generally and his abdomen in particular?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I didn't have any particular concerns about him. I felt that the point that Sophie had raised was explained by the respiratory support that he had received, which was likely blowing a lot of air and gas into both his airway and into his gut.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Thank you, Dr Mayberry. We've seen a statement, we the lawyers in the case, have seen a statement that you made subsequent to the events, within which you deal with two hypothetical issues: one, the issue of free blood in the peritoneum, and the second to do with a liver injury, specifically a subcapsular haematoma. Dealing with them in turn, could you please, in words that we laypeople can understand, explain what free blood in the peritoneum is?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Sure. So the peritoneum is a compartment within which the contents of the abdomen is contained. Blood is not normally found freely within it, so that would be a not usual finding in a healthy child.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: If you were to examine the abdomen and, more particularly, palpate the abdomen of a neonate who had free blood in their peritoneum, what would you expect to discover?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So it is quite unusual to find a child who has free blood within the peritoneum and I have only come across it in a few circumstances. In those circumstances, normally you see a child who is very unwell and often has signs of peritonitis, that is to say inflammation of the lining of that cavity. Therefore they appear to be very unwell and the abdomen is normally fairly firm from my experience.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Thank you. That anticipated presentation, is that consistent or inconsistent with that which you recall observing and feeling with [Baby O] that night shift?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It's not consistent, no.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Thank you. Moving to the second issue, liver injury, more specifically a subcapsular haematoma. Again, in words that we laypeople can understand, what's that?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So the liver is contained within a tissue or a capsule and a subcapsular haematoma is a collection of blood just underneath that capsule.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Thank you. What symptoms would you expect to present to indicate the presence of an injury to that part of a baby's body that would be discoverable upon examination and palpation?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Again, a subcapsular haematoma is quite a rare thing to see. Some of the things that you could think about seeing is a child who is clearly in discomfort from stretching of that capsule by this sort of swelling that's found underneath it. But again it's not something I have great experience in because it's not something that is very commonly found.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: During your examination of [Baby O], did you see anything to indicate that that baby was in discomfort at that point in time?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: None at all.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Can I just take you to a note made by Sophie Ellis.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Mr Murphy, it's behind our tile 105. It's a nursing note and it's a paragraph towards the bottom left of our screen, Mr Murphy. An addendum made at 07.32.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Dr Mayberry, can you see a nursing note on your screen?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, I can.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Towards the bottom of the page, just below a page stamp that says "301", there is an addendum to a note made by Nurse Sophie Ellis made at 07.32. Can you read that to yourself?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Sure, yes. (Pause). I have read it.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Does that accord with your recollection of the examination or does your recollection differ from that in any way?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: No, that is in agreement with my recollection.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Thank you, Dr Mayberry. They are the only questions I wish to ask you in relation to [Baby O]. You may be asked some further questions.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Cross-examination by MR MYERS
Dr Mayberry, you've just been shown a note that was made by Nurse Ellis, haven't you?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Do you actually have an independent recollection of how [Baby O] was at the time that you saw him?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: You will have seen very many children since you examined [Baby O], won't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: And it is some time ago, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: And you have no notes of your own to rely upon, do you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: But you feel still you can recall how he was when you examined him?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Do you remember what time you attended?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Do you recall anything of his blood gas readings at the time, anything at all?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I can only recall them from reading the notes subsequently now. I cannot recall the individual numbers of the blood gas purely from my memory.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Do you recall the abdomen looking "full and slightly loopy", as it says in the note of Sophie Ellis? Do you recall that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I recall the abdomen as being mildly distended.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Do you recall any report of [Baby O] being uncomfortable after the feed?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I recall Sophie contacting me and that being part of her concern, yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: We know, we've got it in our documents, there isn't actually a clinical note for [Baby O] between 10 o'clock in the morning of the 22nd and 9.30 on the morning of the 23rd. Just from your experience, for a baby like this, a triplet like this in a neonatal unit, within the first 1 or 2 days of life, is that standard, there would be a 24-hour period without any clinical note being made?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: If you have a child who has -- where you are not concerned about them, it would not be unusual.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Should you have made a clinical note?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Was it Dr Brearey who questioned you as to why you hadn't made a note after the sad events with [Baby O] had taken place?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Dr Brearey and I spoke after there was a note review, which I believe was a couple of weeks later.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: You've explained you couldn't make a note at the time because you -- were you called away to deal with an emergency elsewhere?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, to the best of my recollection.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Then is it the case that after that, you didn't have time to come back or were you just too busy or did you forget? I'm not suggesting one or the other, I'm just asking you why it was you didn't come back to make the note.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I believe, following on from that, I went to -- there was a medical handover. To the best of my recollection, it was discussed at handover and I said, "I haven't made a note about this", and the team who were going to the neonatal unit said, "Don't worry about it, we're going to go and see him now, so don't worry too much about it".
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: I'm just going to put up, by way of illustration, a note that we have dealing with [Baby O], the note of [Dr D] at tile 4, just to give an example of a note for [Baby O].
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Sure.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: You'll be able to see it or you should be able to see it, Dr Mayberry.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Can you see the note that we can all see on the screen?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: I'm not going to go through all the detail, I'm going to ask Mr Murphy, who's managing the IT display for us, just to pull out so we can see the sort of thing that's on that page of [Dr D]'s notes. Can you see that, Dr Mayberry?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: This is the first page of [Dr D]'s notes and we in the trial have seen a lot of medical notes like this.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Sure.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: When an examination is conducted of a child, of a baby, there are a lot of features that you are meant to go through and confirm and examine, aren't there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Then you can make a record so we can actually see how, in all those different ways, the baby was presenting at the time. That's what it enables us to do, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Did you conduct the sort of examination on [Baby O] that dealt with all the type of features, with fluids and breathing and heart sounds and the like, that we have in a note like this?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: This is a different kind of note. So this is a note which looks at the condition in which [Baby O] was born and subsequently the management that was required to resuscitate [Baby O] when he was born. Therefore, to me, this is a different kind of note to that I would write when I was asked to examine somebody due to a low-level concern.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Yes, I have already said that I wish that I had written a note on it and that that is something that I would have done and I appreciate the point that you're making about writing medical notes. However, not all notes will be quite as detailed as a resuscitation note for a newborn.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: I recognise this is a note, the one we're looking at there, which is made very soon after the time of birth.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: We have also seen, so you know, many notes of babies when they have been reviewed, not just within the first day or two of birth, but at other times, that do contain information like this. Do you accept that does happen?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Um... I... I accept that we write notes and in some detail, yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: All right. We've seen them, so we can gauge what you say about what we have seen. Without actually having the notes, it's very difficult, casting our minds back, to know the various ways in which [Baby O] presented according to the different parts of him that you checked, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Um, it is... I... I'm sorry, I'm not sure how to answer that question. I appreciate I haven't written the notes myself. I have asked somebody, a nurse, to document what was there and I appreciate that that was not written by me. I accept that I -- if I could go back and do it, I would go and write it.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: From your recollection --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Sorry to interrupt you, Mr Myers. Do we still need this on the screen? I think we should see the witness.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Of course. Thank you, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: There we are. Right.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: We've seen, from what Sophie Ellis documents, a reference to [Baby O]'s abdomen and you recall examining that. Do you recall examining him generally?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I recall examining, predominantly focused on his abdomen, but as you reminded me, it was a very long time ago, so my main path of my independent memory relates to his abdomen because at the time when it was discussed -- later on the concern was that he may have had an episode of something like necrotising enterocolitis. That is where my independent memory comes from because I was shocked at his deterioration and his abdomen being the main cause for concern regarding that.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Right. Could you just repeat -- did you say you were shocked at? What did you say?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I was shocked at his deterioration.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: When you were answering questions about the fact of the way in which his abdomen was distended, you said it was no
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: surprise to you when you examined him that it was distended. Do you remember saying that? Just now when you were answering questions.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Sure. If that's what I said, I'll take your word for it, yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: No, I'll help you. It's not to be difficult. You made reference to CPAP and high-flow ventilation.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: High-flow nasal cannula oxygenation, yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Is that Optiflow?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. Sorry, yes. That's the non-brand name for Optiflow.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: So is what you mean that because he was being ventilated in that way, that raises a possibility of air entering down into the gut from the ventilation?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: And that's one reason that an abdomen can distend, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. It's a reason -- it's a very common reason why you may see an abdomen distend in somebody on such ventilation.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: As you say, you have to keep other things in mind because, although that's common, it's important not to just assume that's an end of the matter and not to consider other, more concerning possibilities? It's important, isn't it, to keep your mind open to whatever could lie behind the distension?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Of course, yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: There's one other thing I wanted to ask you about, Dr Mayberry. You were asked about subcapsular haematoma.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: And I think you conceded it's not an area in which you're proposing to deal with it as an expert; that's right, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Sure, yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Just looking at what you have said on the topic, you make reference to:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "It's an area where, when lines are put in through the umbilical cord of a baby, one of the areas they have to travel through is the liver."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And when you made reference to that in your statement, what's the relevance between that and subcapsular haematoma, which is an injury to the liver?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: So I was asked about in which circumstances I had seen that previously.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: And what was it that you'd seen previously?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Injury to the liver from an umbilical venous catheter.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: So something being inserted into the body there, which had gone on to actually go into the liver and penetrate it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Thank you, Dr Mayberry.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Re-examination by MR DRIVER
Just a few topics of re-examination.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Dr Mayberry, you were shown a comprehensive note made by [Dr D], which you accurately identified as a note made upon attendance at the birth of a triplet.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: You half answered the question by saying:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "It's different to the sort of note to be made when examining somebody due to a low level..."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And then you petered out. Could you complete that sentence for us? Due to a low level what, sorry?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Due to a low-level concern.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Thank you. Why do you categorise the concern expressed about [Baby O] as low level?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: There's many reasons to categorise it as a low-level concern. The first and probably most important was that, apart from the fact that his abdomen was mildly distended, there were no other concerning features with it to suggest that he was having another serious kind of problem going on at the time. His observations were within normal limits. There was no concern
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: about him clinically deteriorating or needing further increased ventilation or ventilatory support as you might expect with somebody who's undergoing a serious problem within their gut.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Thank you. You've explained the circumstances as to why you left [Baby O] without making a note. What was the essence of your duty that night?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I'm sorry, maybe you could phrase that somewhat differently, sorry.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Certainly. You were a registrar in the Countess of Chester Hospital; is that right?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Which units were you on call for?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So essentially, I was on call for three different units.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: I was on call for the neonatal -- well, four actually: on call for the neonatal unit; I was on call for, essentially, birthing emergencies or births where support was required for resuscitating children; I was also on call for the general paediatrics wards; and furthermore I was also on call for emergencies involving children within the emergency department, all of which I may have to attend.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Thank you. You were asked questions about your capacity to recall your examination of [Baby O] in the absence of a contemporaneous note.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: How many times in your professional career have you encountered naturally conceived identical triplet boys?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It's very -- it's relatively rare. I'd say probably two or three times.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Of those two or three times, how many times have you had the misfortune to encounter the death of two of those naturally conceived identical triplet boys within a few days of life?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: This is the only occasion.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Does your Lordship have any questions for the witness?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I don't, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Dr Mayberry will be invited back next week to speak of [Baby P].
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: All right. Thank you very much, Dr Mayberry, for coming again tonight. It's quite late in the evening where you are, is it?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, it's 10 o'clock.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Right. You will be required again. At the same time will it be, Mr Driver?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, of course, we will put him on first.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Next week you'll be linking in again. In the meantime, don't talk to anyone about anything to do with this case, please.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: No problem.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Thank you very much indeed.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: My Lord, may I hand over to my learned friend Mr Astbury.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. Whilst that's happening, it is hot in here again today. I was alerted to this before court sat and a request has been made for the temperature to be turned down a bit because we have to strike a happy medium if we can. I, of course, wear clothing that makes it appear hotter to me than those dressed in normal clothing. If you are uncomfortably hot at any time or uncomfortably cold, pass a message to me and I'll do what I can. But I don't think there's actual consensus between you as to whether you want it hotter or colder. I see you nodding. We'll have our breaks as usual so people can get a bit cooler at times. We can't provide individual fans or anything like that to cool you down.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Mr Murphy, please.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (Pause)
Yes, Mr Astbury.
Could I call, please, Dr Katarzyna Cooke.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR KATARZYNA COOKE (affirmed)
Examination-in-chief by MR ASTBURY
Although I'll be asking you questions, and I'm sure very politely you'll be looking at me, if you can make sure you project your voice, please, to the back of the room, we'd be very grateful.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Could we start, please, with your full name?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: My name is Dr Katarzyna Cooke.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: Thank you. Your occupation, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I'm a doctor.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: Thank you. Did you originally train as a doctor in Poland?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, I did.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: For a period of 5 years?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: Where you reached the equivalent of a specialist registrar level?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: Did you then come to the UK?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: Currently I'm employed as a specialty registrar by Burnley Hospital.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: Thank you. You've come along to assist today with your treatment and contact with a baby by the name of [Baby O].
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay, that gives us all an idea of when --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: As a timeline, yes.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: Did you have the assistance, in preparing your statement, of the notes that you made at the hospital?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, I did.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: Is that how the system was supposed to work?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: And had you been advised of any concerns about a particular baby, is that the type of thing you would have made a note about?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, at the start of my ward round.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: Right, thank you. Does the ward round consist of an assessment of all babies on the unit?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, it does.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: And as a consequence of any examination, are the nurses kept up to date with what you find and any changes that are planned?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: Thank you. Is it right that you were one of two SHOs on duty that particular morning?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, from recollection of memory, yes.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: And the other, in this case being you, the neonatal unit and the labour and delivery suite?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: You made a note of your examination of [Baby O], did you?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, I did.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: I wonder if we can have a look at that. There's a screen to your right, doctor, and we will put documents up from time to time, which we hope will assist.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: 121, please, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: If we scroll down, do you recognise the handwriting?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I do, yes.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: You've noted, firstly, his age at birth and then his age at the time you're examining him?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: Is that his birth weight to the right-hand side of that line?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, it is.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: Your writing is very neat, but could you take me through, please, firstly that -- is that no --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I note that there was no nursing concerns and [Baby O]'s observations at that time were normal.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: So would we take it from that that you'd have discussed [Baby O] with his designated nurse --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: -- before the examination?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, I would.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: And any concerns from that designated nurse would be noted at the outset?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, that would be what I would routinely do.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: Do you happen to recall who [Baby O]'s designated nurse was that day?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, we wouldn't make a note of that.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: You've put "observations normal".
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: Is that what you've been told or is that from your --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's good practice to have a look at baby's observations yourself, going through nursing charts and what's been documented over periods from 12 to 24 hours.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: I don't think we need to go to them, but are they the observations chart with heart rate, respiration?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: And would you also be looking at the equipment and the fluid balance chart?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, and temperature.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: You have noted the problems experienced to date by [Baby O], "(1) Prematurity"; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, that's prematurity.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: (2), you have noted he's on Optiflow having been on CPAP yesterday. Then you put a note, "Apnoeas".
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Apnoeas, yes.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: We understand from CPAP on one day, on to Optiflow the next?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: Is that a positive or a negative sign?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's a positive change.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: Thank you. In what way?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Optiflow is a gentler respiratory support that we use as a step down -- and the weaning means -- in babies who are premature and have problems with breathing due to that.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: Thank you. "Presumed sepsis"; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: But you then make a note that -- is that antibiotics stopped --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Stopped.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: -- on 23 June?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: Why was that, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So every baby born prematurely with signs of respiratory distress, by which I mean increased work of breathing or any other problems requiring support with breathing, would be also screened for infection, we call it sepsis.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: It's a routine practice for all the babies in such circumstances. If investigations taken at that time, so infection levels and blood culture, are negative then antibiotics are subsequently discontinued and the suspicion or presumption of sepsis is a resolved problem.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: Okay. So a precautionary step until such time as the blood tests suggest otherwise?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, exactly.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: Thank you. If we go next, please, to ventilation, we've already discussed his Optiflow status. That's 4 litres, is it, in air?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: So no additional oxygen required?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: Is that, "Gas normal"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, the gas was normal.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: What do you mean by gas in that context?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Gas is an investigation, it's a blood investigation, which is obtained by the nursing team mostly, but also can be done by doctor's team, by a prick on baby's heel.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: The result is obtained instantly and gives us an idea on how efficient a baby's breathing is and whether the support that a baby requires at that time is sufficient and also, based on that, whether it can be weaned further or not.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: We've heard a little bit about this and I'm not proposing to go to it, but is that recorded on a blood gas record sheet?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Usually amongst the nursing sheets there would be a special designated sheet with gas records on it.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: And that would include, would it, things like pH, oxygen saturation, lactate?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: Those sort of readings. Thank you. If we go on, please, is that F for feeding?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's F for fluids.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: Thank you. Is that indicating an increase for that particular day?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, it is, from 75ml per kilogram per day to 90ml per kilogram per day.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: Is that suggesting it's via a nasogastric tube?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: And it's donor-expressed breast milk?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: You have noted trace of aspirates?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: Just explain to us the significance of that, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: In babies born prematurely, we usually -- below 34 weeks, if they are born below 34 weeks' gestation we support them in establishing feeds, inserting a nasogastric tube, and then they receive milk of choice through that. Before every feed, the nursing team check the volume of aspirates, if any, and it's --
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: what we do on our doctor's review is we are obliged to check what was the volume of aspirates, if it's trace and done(?) on bilis, that's a reassuring sign.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: So what does trace mean, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: A minimal amount. Usually the nursing team would document it in millilitres, but it's also not uncommon for them to write that it's been a trace or minimal without quantifying the aspirate.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: And would that absence of concerning aspirates have informed the decision to increase the fluids?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Amongst other factors, yes. Basically, what we would look at is baby's fluid balance, feed tolerance, which is one of the things that we look at, also reviewing aspirates, and whether baby is opening bowels, and obviously the examination of the baby on review.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: What do trace aspirates tell you about feed tolerance?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That is good because there is no retention of feed in the stomach in between feeds.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: Thank you. Is that "passed urine" with a tick?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: Is that "bowels open" with a tick?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, it is.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: For medication, we can see caffeine and vitamins?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: And the J, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Jaundice.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: The SBR, the bilirubin levels, is that below the line whereby any intervention is required?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: Thank you. Again if we can scroll down, please, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So that's cranial ultrasound review, which would be a consultant review of the images obtained by a less experienced member of staff.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: Okay. As it happens, we can see, if we go to the next note, it's a note from [Dr B], one of consultants, is that right --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: -- indicating normal appearances on that CRUS? We'll leave [Dr B] to look at that, if necessary.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So overall, please, doctor, having refreshed your memory of all those readings, information and indeed your own physical examination of [Baby O], can you describe to us, please, whether you had any concerns whatsoever about his welfare?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: From the notes, it doesn't appear like I had any concerns about [Baby O], and his clinical course was uncomplicated and he was making good progress.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: Thank you. We mentioned earlier the blood culture. If I could just ask, please, Mr Murphy, to go to page J27105. We can see there --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's blood group, not blood culture.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: That's the start of the report. That gives us the time and date, does it, of the blood, on the first box down?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Is that a later test that you carried out?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So this is blood group and presence of antibodies in a baby, which would be a routine check in all premature babies. That tells us whether a baby is at higher risk of jaundice in their post-natal period. That doesn't tell us about infection.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: I'm going to ask you to look specifically at page 3 of this document.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. That's the result of a blood culture taken on 21 June 2016.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: Is that what you were referring to in --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: -- your note when you said you reached the decision to stop antibiotics?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: Thank you. We can take that down, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: From the notes, did you see that, in fact, despite your examination and findings in respect of [Baby O], he fell ill later that afternoon?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, he did.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: Were you aware that [Dr A], for example, was asked to review him on more than one occasion?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: And on either of those occasions did you discuss the situation with [Dr A]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I would have to refer to the notes. From recollection of memory, yes. If I could see the notes chronologically...
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: If this assists, was there any conversation about Bell's criteria?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. I think from recollection of memory, and a vague recollection of my notes that I've read before coming here, we had a teaching conversation with regards to Bell's criteria, which is criteria used to assess the severity of a condition called necrotising enterocolitis, which is a common complication of prematurity.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: After that training conversation with [Dr A], did you have any more physical contact with [Baby O] that afternoon?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: From recollection of memory, I don't think I had, no.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: Were you aware that at some point [Baby O] required resuscitation?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, I was, and unfortunately I again cannot remember, but I had assisted with CPR in one of the babies that fell poorly during that period. I can't remember which one was that.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: All right. You initially provided a statement to the police concerning your notes and your recollection of [Baby O]. Were you asked to provide a second statement dealing with a specific issue with relation to that examination?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, I was.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: Were you asked -- perhaps if we could put tile 121 back up, please, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's really your entry regarding your examination of [Baby O]'s abdomen that I would like to concentrate on, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: You have already told us you found nothing that caused you any concern during the course of that examination.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: Were you invited to revisit that in light of the presence of a haematoma discovered on [Baby O]'s liver?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, I was.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: You were asked whether your examination and what you recall of your examination was what you would expect, whether it was consistent with that injury being -- that haematoma being present at the time of your examination; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: What is your view of your examination in comparison to the presence of that haematoma?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So examination wouldn't -- in my experience, examination at that time would not suggest and review of observations would not suggest anything like a haematoma being present at that time.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: Okay. What would you, in your experience, have expected on examination if a haematoma had been present in [Baby O]'s liver at that time?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: My understanding of a haematoma is a collection of blood that happens either acutely or in a chronic manner. If that was an acute concern I would have seen -- my review wouldn't be normal, by which I mean the observations would suggest that baby is undergoing deterioration as opposed to normal examination, normal observations and no concerns from either the night team or the nursing team taking care of the baby at that time.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: You described two possibilities, was it acute and one other. Was it --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Chronic.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Just explain those two, please.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: My understanding of acute is a bleed happening then and there for whatever reason at that time. Chronic would be slow build-up of blood collection within the area we call haematoma.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: All right. I think you divided your answer, if I can put it this way, into two parts. Firstly, the physical examination --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: -- and also the other signs?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: And we have heard that often it's a collective view of everything that's going on that informs the doctors?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: So what would you have expected from your physical examination, first?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: From physical examination, I would expect a baby who's looking unwell, is pale, clammy, has a tender abdomen and a distended abdomen.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: Okay. None of which you've noted in your note at 09.30?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: COOKE

blocks.text: And I've not shown you the blood gas records or the observations, we can if necessary. But generally, what other signs would you be looking for to add to that concern?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Increase in oxygen requirement or need to escalate the respiratory support that the baby was on at that time.
blocks.speaker: COOKE
